job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Colin Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an analyst in my first job at Harlow & Reed, a mid-size consultancy in the city, and I live in a rented flat with two friends from university. Days are a mix: building market models in a spreadsheet, running data through a couple of AI tools, and turning it into slides for whichever manager is shouting loudest that day. I finished my business analytics degree top of my cohort, with internships at a retailer and a bank. My parents run a convenience store on Maple Road, so I grew up behind a till doing the stock count, and I still go home on Sundays and fix whatever's broken in their system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine, they were overselling it, and I'd probably be one of the few who isn't surprised. I'd tell my manager that the tools I already use are a decent time-saver and that's about it. Online I'd laugh at the people who said it would end the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'm okay. I use these tools every day and I know where they fall over. AI tools are great at the first draft and rubbish at knowing which question the client should actually be asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, work on becoming the person who gets the first draft right in an hour, not a day. I'd also keep fixing my parents' shop system on Sundays, because it's fun and I learn from it. And I'd put £200 a month into an index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relaxed. It's nice for once to not have a plot twist. I'd enjoy it while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or worry in your own life would stay exactly the same even if nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents' shop. Margins are thin and the big supermarket opened half a mile away, and they're not getting any younger. That's a worry no AI helps or hurts much, though I'd like to think I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your week is routine screen work that even a small change could touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot of my day is slides and models, so yes, the small tools already touch it. If everyone gets another 20 percent faster, the firm needs fewer of us for the same projects. I'd watch the utilisation number on my timesheet.

say: I'd say they were **overselling** it and I'm not surprised.
I'd tell my manager the tools are a decent **time-saver**.
I'd laugh online at the end-of-the-world **predictions**.
think: I know where the tools **fall over**, so I'm okay.
They're good at drafts and bad at the right **question**.
My parents' **shop** worries me more than my job.
do: Learn to get a first draft right in an **hour**, not a day.

Put **£200 a month** into an index fund.
feel: **Relaxed**, with no plot twist for once.
A small **tug** about my parents' margins.

fieldNote: His calm comes from **daily use** and knowing the tools' limits.
The real worry is his parents' **shop** and a nearby supermarket.
Notes utilisation, the **billing metric**, as the place where speed gains bite.

steps.text: Get a first draft right in an hour using the AI tools
Put £200 a month into an index fund
Keep delivering models on time for my manager

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming and the sensible move is to get good at it. At work I'd offer to run a lunch session on prompts and checks, and I'd tell the grads who aren't using it to start. Online I'd post some honest tips about where the tools break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd say consulting juniors are directly in the path. The data work and first slides are what the tools do now. Firms like mine sell hours, and when the hours shrink, the first people to feel it are the ones who bill the cheapest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move toward the part of the job that sells, like talking to clients and framing the problem. I'd also build a small internal tool that checks the AI's numbers, because that's useful to my team. And I'd start the side idea I've had for a year: a simple analytics service for small shops, starting with my parents'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a little hungry. There's a bit of fear in it, because the entry job is the one at risk, but I like the pace. I'd rather be early than neat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Think of a task you did last week. Which part would software take over first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first slide deck and the data clean-up. I did a market sizing last month that took two days, and I could do it in a morning now. What stays is picking which numbers matter and defending them in a room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your manager do differently about hiring people at your level?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd cut the graduate intake and promote faster the ones who stay. A manager called Priyanka said last month that the target is each person handling two projects, not one. I'd ask for three and see what happens.

I'd post tips online about where the tools **break**.

do: Move toward **client talk** and framing problems.

Start the **analytics** service for small shops, beginning with my parents'.

S1.quote: Firms like mine sell hours, and when the hours shrink, the first people to feel it are the ones who bill the cheapest.
fieldNote: He treats the change as a **market** and tries to sell into it.
Recognises that **cheapest billers** get hit first, which includes him.

steps.text: Run a lunchtime session on prompts and checks for graduates
Offer shop analytics to five small shops on Maple Road
Build a script that audits the AI's numbers for my team
Ask Priyanka to put me on client calls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say hold on, that's too fast for everyone, and the people who run banks and governments aren't ready. At work I'd keep my nerve and say we should be the firm that works out how to use it. Online I'd be blunt about the risk that a lot of jobs go at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be properly worried. If AI does any thinking job better and cheaper, consulting is among the first to go, and I'm a 24-year-old analyst with a degree in exactly that. The one thing I'm good at is what the machine does best, and it will get cheaper every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for ownership. I'd take the shop analytics idea and turn it into a real business with five paying clients, using the tools to do the work of a team. I'd cut costs hard, save £500 a month, and push my parents to automate the shop's ordering before the supermarket squeezes them further.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired and sleepless. Part of me finds it thrilling, which is a weird thing to say. It's like standing on the edge of something very big, and I might fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Say it's the day the announcement is made. What do you tell the people close to you that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with my parents and say the shop can be the first customer for my project. Dad would say don't gamble your job, and I'd say the job is the gamble. We'd both be right in a way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, what happens to the money you owe and the money you've saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the student loan going at the minimum and hold six months of cash. If the firm lets me go, I'd have a runway. I'd also sell my laptop upgrade plans and stop the gym, small things that add up.

I'd say our firm should be the one that works out the **new way**.
I'd be blunt online about a lot of jobs going **at once**.
think: Consulting is among the first to go, and I have a degree in **exactly that**.

The job itself may be the **gamble**.
do: Turn the shop idea into a business with **five** paying clients.
Save **£500 a month** and cut costs hard.
Push my parents to **automate** the shop's ordering.
S2.quote: The one thing I'm good at is what the machine does best, and it will get cheaper every month.
fieldNote: Anxious but **energised**; he answers fear with building.

His parents' **shop** becomes both safety and first customer.

steps.text: Sign five paying small-shop clients for my analytics service
Save £500 a month to hold six months of cash
Set up automatic ordering in my parents' shop
Stop the gym and buy no new gear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty of time to build something if you start now. I'd tell my colleagues to take side projects seriously and learn the tools well. I'd also say that the firms that treat staff well in the transition will keep the good ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel more upside than downside. By 2031 I'd be 27 and could have my own small business running. Five years is long enough to build a business that earns, and short enough that I can't afford to wait for permission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm for two more years to learn how big clients think, then leave. I'd use that time to grow the shop analytics side into a company with ten clients. I'd save £400 a month and keep my spending low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired, with a more settled edge than the two-year case. I like having a clock. It's motivating rather than scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes about your plan with 5 years instead of 2?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd hustle and hold cash. With five I'd build the machine and pick the right clients. It changes the question from "how do I survive" to "what do I want to own".

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you do you think sees this coming, and who doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My manager Priyanka sees it, and so do two or three of the juniors. Most of the partners think it's a cost-saver. My parents don't think about it, but they'd say the shop will always have customers, and I'm not so sure.

say: I'd say five years is plenty of time to **build** something.
I'd tell colleagues to take **side projects** seriously.
I'd say firms that treat staff well will keep the **good ones**.
think: By 2031 I could have my own small **business** running.
do: Stay two years at the firm, then **leave** to run my own.
Grow the shop analytics side to **ten clients**.
Save **£400 a month**, keeping spending low.
feel: Wired but more **settled** than at two years.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to build a business that earns, and short enough that I can't afford to wait for permission.
fieldNote: Time shifts his question from **surviving** to owning something.
Sees **partners** as seeing only cost savings.
His **parents** are the people he is unsure about.

steps.text: Grow my shop analytics work to ten paying clients
Leave the consultancy in two years to run it full time
Put £150 a month into the index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, and I'd treat it like a start-up: plan, test, adjust. I'd tell friends there's room to be bold. I'd also say that the next generation will find it harder, so let's not pull the ladder up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd feel good, with a few worries. By 2036 I'd be 32 and could have a company or a senior role. I'd still be thinking about my parents' retirement and whether the shop survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work for two years, then start my own firm, hire two or three juniors and teach them properly. I'd use AI heavily and learn the next wave of tools as they arrive. I'd invest regularly and help my parents decide how and when to sell the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. It feels like an open door. I'd just need to walk through it before someone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, what would you start now that you wouldn't with 2 years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade lets me build something and then hire the juniors the market stopped hiring, which is the part of this I'd actually enjoy. It's a chance to be the manager I'd have liked to have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At 32, what do you hope your working life looks like, and what could stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 32 I'd like to have a small company with a handful of staff. What could stop me is a recession, a cash crunch, or the big firms bundling everything into one machine that undercuts all of us.

say: I'd say ten years is a long **runway**, so treat it like a start-up.
I'd tell friends there's room to be **bold**.
I'd say we mustn't **pull the ladder up**.
think: By 2036 I'd be 32 with a **company** or a senior role.
I'd still think about my parents' **retirement**.
do: Work two years, then start my own **firm** and hire juniors.
Learn the next wave of **tools** as they arrive.

fieldNote: He wants to **hire** juniors, a clear sign of his values.

Move my firm's reporting onto automated AI tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I wouldn't have time to build anything. What would help is cheap access to the tools for small businesses, some rules so big firms don't just swallow everything, and a safety net so people can try things without being ruined.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say people think I'm a tech optimist, and I am, but I worry about a lot of people being left. I'm fine because I like the machines, and the fact that I'm fine is the problem, because most of my friends don't. I'd want someone to take that seriously.

headlineQuote: I'm fine because I like the machines, and the fact that I'm fine is the problem, because most of my friends don't.
portrait: Colin is a **22-year-old** consultancy analyst, top of his class, who uses AI daily and builds on the side.
His parents run a **convenience store**, which is both his worry and his test case.
He is centrist, blames **no side**, and answers every threat by building something he can own.
He is calm in slow worlds, **anxious** at two years but energised, and hopes to hire juniors later.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because there would be no time to build anything of his own.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap tools for **small businesses**, rules against big-firm swallowing, and a safety net for risk-taking.
